why: Breaking an ant trail and watching it mend helps your child test a prediction and explain how many small actions build one pattern.
teaser: Follow a line of ants to a crumb, then find the invisible scent road, break it, and see why the shortest trail always wins.
title: How an Ant Trail Works
question: How does every ant in a line know the way to the food?
idea: A scout ant that finds food paints the way home with a scent called a pheromone. Other ants smell it with their antennae, follow it and add more. The shortest road gets the most scent, and scent that nobody renews fades away.

curiosity.intro: Start with a line of ants on a patio. Then meet the scout, break the trail, race two bridges, watch a new trail grow and visit a rainforest ant highway.
curiosity.carryForward: Next time you see ants in a line, look for where the trail began and guess where it ends.

questions.question: How does the first ant mark the way?
questions.notice: Find the crumb in the ant's jaws and the tip of its body touching the paper.
questions.say: The first ant to find food is a scout. On her way home, she dabs the tip of her body on the ground again and again. Each dab leaves a little scent called a pheromone. Ants smell with their two antennae, so the others can follow her invisible road straight to the food.
questions.try: Put one crumb near some ants outside. Watch for the first ant to find it. Does she eat it there, or carry it home?

questions.question: What happens if you wipe the trail?
questions.notice: Find the shiny wiped stripe and the ants turning in small loops at its edge.
questions.say: The ants stop! Wiping removes the scent, so the road is gone right there. The ants wave their antennae and wander in loops, searching. Soon one ant finds the scent on the far side, crosses, and leaves new scent behind her. The line joins up again.
questions.try: Find a busy ant trail on a path. Wipe a damp cloth across one spot, then step back. How long until the ants cross again?

questions.question: Why do ants pick the shortest road?
questions.notice: Compare the crowded short bridge with the long bridge that has only a few ants.
questions.say: Nobody measures. Ants on the short bridge get back sooner, so they add scent to it more often. More scent pulls in more ants, and they add even more. The scent on the long bridge slowly fades away. Soon almost every ant uses the short road. Scientists tried this with real bridges.
questions.try: Put two crumbs outside, one near the ants and one far away. Which crumb gets a busy trail first?

questions.question: How big can an ant trail get?
questions.notice: Find the bare, swept path and the leaf pieces held up like little sails.
questions.say: Leafcutter ants clear their trails of twigs and leaves, so they become real little roads. Thousands of ants carry leaf bits home to feed a fungus garden. Sometimes army ants get lost following a trail that loops in a circle, and march round and round. People call that an ant mill.
questions.try: Draw an ant trail from your door to a crumb. Then draw a shorter road. Which one would the ants pick, and why?

beats.title: Wipe the trail
beats.passage: Here is a test. Wipe a damp cloth across one spot on the trail. The ants reach the wiped stripe and stop! They wave their antennae and wander in little loops. The scent road is broken there. Soon one ant crosses and leaves fresh scent, and the line joins up again.

beats.title: The short road wins
beats.passage: Here is a clue. Scientists once gave ants two bridges to some honey, one short and one long. At first, ants used both. But ants on the short bridge got back sooner, so they added scent there more often. That trail grew stronger and pulled in more ants. Meanwhile, the scent on the long bridge faded away.
beats.prompt: Why did the short bridge get more scent?

foldable.heading: The short road wins
foldable.body: Ants on the short bridge got back sooner. They added scent more often, so that trail grew strong. The long one faded.

beats.title: A brand-new trail
beats.passage: Later, the little one sets a sugar cube near the line. Before long, a new line of ants branches off toward it. Now the guess changes. No ant is the leader. math.title: Ant trail counts
math.intro: Compare and round pretend counts of ants, crumbs and bridge crossings.

tasks.prompt: Little Wonderer counts 61 ants on the patio trail and 16 ants near the flower pot. Put >, <, or = in the circle. What is the greater count (or the shared count if equal)?
tasks.hint: Compare tens first, then ones. When both counts match, use = and give that shared count.
tasks.worked: 61 > 16. Compare the tens first, so the greater count is 61.
tasks.label: TASK 1

tasks.prompt: In a pretend count, the nest gets 29 crumbs in the morning and 92 crumbs in the afternoon. Put >, <, or = in the circle. What is the greater count (or the shared count if equal)?
tasks.hint: Compare tens first, then ones. When both counts match, use = and give that shared count.
tasks.worked: 29 < 92. Compare the tens first, so the greater count is 92.
tasks.label: TASK 2

tasks.prompt: The big one counts 67 ants waiting at the wiped stripe. What is 67 rounded to the nearest ten?
tasks.hint: Look at the ones. With 5 or more, go up to the next ten; otherwise go down.
tasks.worked: 67 has 7 ones, so round up to 70.
tasks.label: TASK 3

tasks.prompt: In a pretend count, 58 ants cross the short bridge in one minute, and 58 cross it the next minute. Put >, <, or = in the circle. What is the greater count (or the shared count if equal)?
tasks.hint: Compare tens first, then ones. When both counts match, use = and give that shared count.
tasks.worked: 58 = 58. Both counts match, so the shared count is 58.
tasks.label: TASK 4

tasks.prompt: The little one watches 34 ants march to the sugar cube. What is 34 rounded to the nearest ten?
tasks.hint: Look at the ones. With 5 or more, go up to the next ten; otherwise go down.
tasks.worked: 34 has 4 ones, so round down to 30.
tasks.label: TASK 5

tasks.prompt: In a pretend count, 85 leafcutter ants carry leaves past one fern. What is 85 rounded to the nearest ten?
tasks.hint: Look at the ones. With 5 or more, go up to the next ten; otherwise go down.
tasks.worked: 85 has 5 ones, so round up to 90.
tasks.label: TASK 6

math.extension: Choose one problem and draw the tens as sticks and the ones as dots to check.
math.printNote: Show your thinking with numbers, marks, or words.
math.parentNote: Three two-digit comparisons and three nearest-ten roundings. The numbers are for practice, not real ant counts.
math.answerKeyIntro: Compare tens first, then ones. For rounding, 5 or more ones rounds up.

poem.title: The Ant Parade
lines: Little Wonderer found a parade on the stone:
a ring of black ants, and not one walked alone.
Each ant sniffed the trail of the ant just ahead
and went round and around where the last ant had led.
“They’re stuck,” said the big one. “Each ant trusts its nose,
and the nose says go round, so around the ring goes.
There’s a crumb in the middle, a feast for a queen,
but they never look up. It’s the strangest I’ve seen.”
“I’ll fix it!” the little one said with a grin,
then stepped to the end of the ring and fell in.
“Just follow me out, little ants! Here we go!”
Then off round the crumb, nice and steady and slow.
Round went the leader past supper and night.
Big Wonderer called, “Are you leading them right?”
“I think so,” came softly, “but I’m not really sure.
I’ve been sniffing this ant for an hour or more!”
